title: Infrastructure pillars
prompt_markdown: Which set contains the three infrastructure pillars introduced in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Deployment, testing, and monitoring

options.label: B
options.text: Compute, storage, and network

options.label: C
options.text: Development, testing, and production

options.label: D
options.text: Applications, users, and source code

grader_markdown: Compute executes workloads, storage retains data, and networking connects resources. The alternatives describe activities, environments, or application-level concerns rather than the three infrastructure pillars.

title: Declarative configuration
prompt_markdown: Which statement best describes a declarative infrastructure definition?

options.label: A
options.text: It records every command an administrator previously executed.

options.label: B
options.text: It specifies the exact sequence of operations for every starting state.

options.label: C
options.text: It describes the desired state, while automation determines how to reach it.

options.label: D
options.text: It guarantees that every operation can run in parallel.

grader_markdown: A declarative definition expresses the intended state. Automation determines the operations needed from the declaration and actual state. Declarative syntax alone does not remove dependencies or guarantee parallel execution.

title: Idempotence
prompt_markdown: An automation run has successfully reached the desired state. Its inputs and the relevant external state then remain unchanged. What should a second idempotent run do?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the managed state unchanged because it already satisfies the declaration.

options.label: B
options.text: Recreate all resources to prove they can be recreated.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip checking the current state and report success.

options.label: D
options.text: Add another copy of each declared resource.

grader_markdown: Once the desired state is satisfied, repeating an idempotent operation under unchanged relevant conditions should cause no further managed-state changes. Checking the current state is compatible with idempotence; doing nothing without checking does not establish correctness.

title: Cloud service models
prompt_markdown: A team moves from managing virtual machines under IaaS to a managed application platform under PaaS. Which responsibility would typically move towards the provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Deciding the application's business requirements

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining the team's application source code

options.label: C
options.text: Choosing which application features to release

options.label: D
options.text: Maintaining more of the underlying operating system and runtime platform

grader_markdown: PaaS typically transfers more operating-system and runtime-platform maintenance to the provider. The exact boundary depends on the service. The application team still owns its business requirements and application code.

title: Version-controlled infrastructure definitions
prompt_markdown: Which pair of benefits best explains how version-controlling infrastructure definitions helps a team deliver changes reliably?

options.label: A
options.text: It preserves change history and makes reverting a definition sufficient to restore deleted application data.

options.label: B
options.text: It provides a shared definition and keeps running infrastructure synchronized whenever a change is committed.

options.label: C
options.text: It makes proposed changes reviewable and records who changed the intended configuration and why.

options.label: D
options.text: It makes environment differences visible and makes validation unnecessary after a change is approved.

grader_markdown: Review before application can catch mistakes, and a traceable history helps explain and investigate changes. Version control alone neither applies changes nor restores deleted data; reviewed changes still need validation.

title: Configuration drift
prompt_markdown: Two servers were created from the same definition. An administrator changes a managed setting manually on one server. Which description and response best address the situation?

options.label: A
options.text: The server has drifted from the declared state; compare the difference and either restore the approved setting or review and update the definition.

options.label: B
options.text: The definition has become obsolete; copy the changed setting into it and apply it to the other server without further review.

options.label: C
options.text: The servers are still consistent because they share an original definition; record the manual change only in an operational log.

options.label: D
options.text: The difference is necessarily a fault; rebuild both servers immediately without checking why the setting was changed.

grader_markdown: Drift is a difference between actual managed state and intended state. Investigate it before reconciliation: an unauthorized change may need reversal, while a legitimate change should be reviewed and recorded in the definition. A shared origin does not guarantee continued consistency.

title: Mutable and immutable infrastructure
prompt_markdown: A server needs an operating-system configuration change and stores application data that must survive the update. Which plan correctly distinguishes mutable and immutable approaches?

options.label: A
options.text: A mutable update replaces the server; an immutable update modifies the existing server while preserving its identity.

options.label: B
options.text: Both approaches modify the existing server; the immutable approach additionally records the change in version control.

options.label: C
options.text: A mutable update changes the existing server; an immutable update replaces it and recreates persistent data from the infrastructure definition.

options.label: D
options.text: A mutable update changes the existing server; an immutable update replaces it and preserves persistent data separately or through a verified migration.

grader_markdown: Mutable updates change an existing instance. Immutable updates replace it with an instance prepared from the updated definition or image. Persistent application data needs separate storage or a verified transfer/recovery process; infrastructure definitions do not generally contain that data.

title: Separating infrastructure and server configuration
prompt_markdown: A deployment needs networks and virtual machines, plus software and service configuration inside those machines. Which organization best separates responsibilities while keeping the deployment coordinated?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain each environment as a complete independent copy so changes to shared configuration never affect another environment.

options.label: B
options.text: Separate resource provisioning from server configuration, pass required resource information between them, and review each concern independently.

options.label: C
options.text: Put provisioning and configuration in separate repositories and rely on operators to keep their connection details synchronized.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep only resource provisioning in code and document the manual software setup as the interface between the two responsibilities.

grader_markdown: Provisioning establishes resources and connectivity; server configuration establishes software, files, and service state. Clear boundaries with explicit information flow support focused review and reuse. Separate repositories are optional and do not by themselves keep dependencies synchronized.

title: Dependencies and changing resource information
prompt_markdown: An application server requires a network. A later configuration step needs the server's assigned address, which may change when the server is replaced. The team currently copies that address into several files. Which design best preserves both dependency order and current connection information?

options.label: A
options.text: Represent network-to-server and server-to-configuration dependencies explicitly, and derive the connection address from the current server output.

options.label: B
options.text: Number the definition files in deployment order, and retain the original address as a default in each configuration file.

options.label: C
options.text: Start all stages together, and retry configuration against the previously recorded address until the server becomes reachable.

options.label: D
options.text: Create the network and server in order, and let each configuration stage maintain its own reviewed copy of the assigned address.

grader_markdown: Explicit dependencies identify what must exist or be known before another step can proceed. Passing current resource outputs avoids stale, duplicated addresses after replacement. File names alone do not encode those resource relationships, and correct ordering alone does not keep copied values current.

title: Shared definitions and environment differences
prompt_markdown: Development and production use copied infrastructure definitions. They should share an application structure, but production needs greater capacity. Independent edits have introduced differences whose purpose is unclear. Which approach best preserves legitimate differences and prevents accidental divergence?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep independent definitions and periodically copy production over development, treating production capacity as the shared baseline.

options.label: B
options.text: Require identical definitions and values everywhere, recording production capacity changes only in an operational checklist.

options.label: C
options.text: Share the common structure, keep environment values explicit, and review existing differences against intended state before validating future changes.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a shared definition, permit manual environment-specific changes after deployment, and review only changes to the shared definition.

grader_markdown: A shared definition captures the common structure, while explicit environment values retain intended capacity differences. Compare definitions and actual state with the agreed design, then review and validate changes. Identical values are not required, and undocumented manual exceptions undermine the shared source of truth.

title: Image and running machine
prompt_markdown: What is the relationship between a machine image and a virtual machine?

options.label: A
options.text: The image is the live machine's current CPU and memory usage.

options.label: B
options.text: One image can initialize multiple VM instances, which can later develop different state.

options.label: C
options.text: Every image can initialize only one VM.

options.label: D
options.text: Launching a VM automatically updates the source image whenever the VM changes.

grader_markdown: An image provides the starting state for multiple instances. The instances can change independently after launch; those changes do not automatically rewrite the image.

title: Image building and deployment
prompt_markdown: What distinguishes building a machine image from deploying machines based on that image?

options.label: A
options.text: Building an image automatically replaces every running machine.

options.label: B
options.text: Deployment modifies the shared source image whenever an instance changes.

options.label: C
options.text: Building an image removes the need for any instance-specific configuration.

options.label: D
options.text: Building creates a reusable starting artifact; deployment creates running instances from it.

grader_markdown: Image building prepares a reusable artifact. Deployment uses that artifact to create running instances. Producing a new image does not automatically update existing machines or eliminate instance-specific initialization.

title: Rebuildability
prompt_markdown: The lecture describes a problematic form of a "golden image." What makes that example an anti-pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: The image was modified manually and cannot be reliably recreated from a maintained build definition.

options.label: B
options.text: The organization uses a shared base image.

options.label: C
options.text: The image has been tested before use.

options.label: D
options.text: The image is generated by an automated build pipeline.

grader_markdown: The problem is hidden manual changes and the lack of a maintained, repeatable creation process. A shared baseline or an automated, rebuildable image is not inherently an anti-pattern, even if the team calls it a golden image.

title: Image compatibility
prompt_markdown: A team wants to use the same machine baseline on two virtualization platforms and on different processor architectures. Which assumption is sound?

options.label: A
options.text: Any machine image can boot unchanged on every platform and processor architecture.

options.label: B
options.text: Matching the application's name guarantees that its machine image is compatible.

options.label: C
options.text: The team must check platform and architecture compatibility and may need separate image variants.

options.label: D
options.text: Only disk size determines whether the image can boot.

grader_markdown: Machine images must be compatible with the destination platform and processor architecture. A common intended baseline can require different artifacts or formats for different targets; the exact requirements depend on the target platforms.

title: Stock and custom images
prompt_markdown: An organization starts every server from a supplied stock image and repeats the same security and software setup at launch. What is the strongest reason to maintain a custom image?

options.label: A
options.text: A custom image captures live application data, so it replaces the need for separate data backups.

options.label: B
options.text: A custom image contains a tested organizational baseline, reducing repeated setup while still requiring maintenance.

options.label: C
options.text: A custom image incorporates future security fixes automatically, so its original build definition can remain unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: A custom image removes environment differences, so all settings and machine identities should be embedded in it.

grader_markdown: A stock image is a supplied starting point. A custom image adds selected software and configuration, providing a tested baseline and reducing repeated initialization. It still requires maintenance, instance-specific settings, and separate protection of persistent data.

title: Build time and boot time
prompt_markdown: A fleet needs the same monitoring software on every machine, but each instance needs a distinct identity and environment-specific connection settings. Which division of work best fits image building and first-start initialization?

options.label: A
options.text: Embed the monitoring software and one shared machine identity in the image; change environment settings manually after launch.

options.label: B
options.text: Install everything at first start because reusable images cannot contain configured software.

options.label: C
options.text: Embed all production connection settings in every image; use first-start initialization only to check whether the machine boots.

options.label: D
options.text: Prepare the shared monitoring software in the image; supply instance identity and environment settings during first-start initialization.

grader_markdown: Build-time work becomes part of a reusable image; first-start initialization can supply values specific to an instance or environment. Other divisions may be valid, but this one directly separates the stable shared baseline from the varying inputs. First-start initialization alone is not ongoing reconciliation.

title: Containers and virtual machines
prompt_markdown: Which statement correctly compares a typical Linux container with a virtual machine and identifies a consequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Containers normally share the host kernel, while VMs run guest kernels; a workload requiring a different kernel may need a VM.

options.label: B
options.text: Containers and VMs each boot their own kernel, so they provide the same kernel isolation boundary.

options.label: C
options.text: Containers share the host kernel, so they cannot isolate processes or files from other containers.

options.label: D
options.text: VMs run guest kernels, so any VM image can run unchanged on every processor architecture and hypervisor.

grader_markdown: Typical Linux containers share a host kernel while isolating aspects of their execution environment. A VM has a guest kernel over virtualized hardware. Kernel sharing affects compatibility and isolation; neither approach guarantees that arbitrary images work on every platform.

title: Snapshot and rebuildable definition
prompt_markdown: A team has a snapshot of a working server but no maintained definition of how it was configured. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The snapshot records the intended configuration process, so future changes can be reviewed directly from its creation history.

options.label: B
options.text: The snapshot is unsuitable for recovery because only a rebuildable definition can restore a machine's state.

options.label: C
options.text: The snapshot may restore captured state, but a maintained definition is still needed to review and deliberately reproduce the configuration process.

options.label: D
options.text: The snapshot proves future builds will match the server, provided the same stock image name is selected each time.

grader_markdown: A snapshot captures state at a point in time, within its scope and consistency limits. It can support restoration but does not explain the intended build process or make hidden manual changes reviewable. Rebuildable definitions and data backups serve different purposes.

title: Organizing an image family
prompt_markdown: Web-server and database-server images share a security baseline but need different software. Their separate build definitions contain copied baseline steps, and a policy update reached only one copy. Which plan best addresses both organization and rollout?

options.label: A
options.text: Build one image with both workloads installed; apply a baseline change to whichever running servers currently need it.

options.label: B
options.text: Reuse a common baseline with separate workload definitions; rebuild affected images, validate policy and workload behavior, then deliberately replace affected machines.

options.label: C
options.text: Reuse a common baseline with separate workload definitions; committing its new version also updates existing images and running machines.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep the copied baseline steps and review each copy; validate only the baseline definition before replacing machines with existing images.

grader_markdown: A shared baseline reduces inconsistent copies while workload-specific definitions preserve useful differences. Updating source does not update existing artifacts or instances: affected images must be rebuilt, tested, and deliberately rolled out. Validation should cover both the policy and the workloads.

title: Reproducible builds and immutable updates
prompt_markdown: A version-controlled image build always selects the latest base image and packages. The team wants to reproduce an approved version and later roll out a deliberately patched version. Which plan meets both goals?

options.label: A
options.text: Re-run the same source revision with latest inputs; update existing servers in place and call the unchanged source an immutable release.

options.label: B
options.text: Record the approved base image but continue selecting latest packages; replace all machines and recreate their application data from the build definition.

options.label: C
options.text: Control both base and package versions; patch running machines manually and rely on their original image for future replacements.

options.label: D
options.text: Record and retain approved base and package artifacts; build and validate a patched image, check replacement instances, and preserve persistent data during rollout.

grader_markdown: Version-controlled instructions do not freeze external inputs such as base images and packages. Reproduction requires controlled versions and available artifacts. An immutable update builds and validates a new image, replaces instances deliberately, and protects persistent data through suitable storage or a verified migration/recovery process.

title: Inventory
prompt_markdown: What is the main purpose of an inventory in server configuration management?

options.label: A
options.text: To store a complete binary snapshot of every server

options.label: B
options.text: To replace all reusable configuration definitions

options.label: C
options.text: To identify managed hosts and groups and associate relevant targeting information

options.label: D
options.text: To record only the operations that previously failed

grader_markdown: An inventory identifies target hosts and groups and can associate relevant information with them. It supports selecting the appropriate targets for configuration; it is not a complete backup of their state.

title: Partial state management
prompt_markdown: An automation system manages only the resources explicitly declared to it. Its declaration requires a web service but says nothing about an unrelated package installed manually. What should you expect after a successful run?

options.label: A
options.text: The unrelated package can remain because it is outside the declared scope.

options.label: B
options.text: Every package not named in the declaration is automatically removed.

options.label: C
options.text: The machine is necessarily recreated from a stock image.

options.label: D
options.text: Success proves that every aspect of the machine matches a complete baseline.

grader_markdown: The system in the question manages explicitly declared resources. A resource outside that scope is not automatically declared absent, so unmanaged state can remain even after successful configuration.

title: Reusable configuration units
prompt_markdown: What is the strongest reason to organize server configuration into reusable units for common setup, web services, and databases?

options.label: A
options.text: It guarantees that all configuration actions can run simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: It makes each unit independent of every other resource and input.

options.label: C
options.text: It removes the need to test how the units work together.

options.label: D
options.text: It groups related responsibilities so they can be understood, reused, and maintained separately.

grader_markdown: Grouping related responsibilities creates units that can be understood, reused, and maintained. Such units can still have dependencies and need integration testing; splitting files does not guarantee independence or parallelism.

title: Configuration values and shared logic
prompt_markdown: Development and production use the same service configuration logic but need different capacity values. Which organization best supports reuse and makes the intended differences clear?

options.label: A
options.text: Copy the full logic for each environment and edit the copies independently.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep shared logic reusable and supply explicit environment-specific values through a documented configuration scheme.

options.label: C
options.text: Hide the production values inside unrelated shared configuration files.

options.label: D
options.text: Require both environments to have identical capacity so no values differ.

grader_markdown: Shared logic plus explicit environment values preserves reuse and makes intentional differences reviewable. A documented configuration scheme makes the effective values understandable; copying whole definitions or hiding overrides makes divergence harder to control.

title: Grouping by responsibility
prompt_markdown: Web, database, and batch-processing servers all need a common baseline but different workload configuration. Which organization expresses both requirements with the least duplicated baseline logic?

options.label: A
options.text: Maintain a complete baseline copy for every workload group so each team can change it independently.

options.label: B
options.text: Apply every configuration unit to every server and let operators disable the unwanted services afterward.

options.label: C
options.text: Apply one reusable baseline to the fleet and select workload-specific units through the corresponding host groups.

options.label: D
options.text: Use workload groups only for connection settings and put all server configuration into one sequence applied to every host.

grader_markdown: Grouping selects the appropriate targets; reusable units define the configuration to apply. Composing a common baseline with workload-specific units avoids both duplicated baseline logic and installation of every workload on every host. No particular inventory syntax or folder layout is required.

title: Desired state and operational actions
prompt_markdown: A service is already running and its relevant configuration has not changed. How does declaring that it should be running differ from requesting a restart on every automation run?

options.label: A
options.text: The desired-state declaration can leave it running undisturbed; an unconditional restart requests another operation and can cause unnecessary disruption.

options.label: B
options.text: Both requests must stop and start it again, because automation cannot confirm a running state without restarting.

options.label: C
options.text: The desired-state declaration starts it only on the first deployment; the restart request is the only way to recover it after a later failure.

options.label: D
options.text: The restart request becomes a no-op after its first success, even if the automation explicitly requests it on every run.

grader_markdown: A running-state declaration describes a condition that may already hold. A restart request describes an operation. Repeated execution can therefore leave a healthy service undisturbed with the first approach and disrupt it with the second. Relevant changes can still justify a restart.

title: Responding to configuration changes
prompt_markdown: Several compatible configuration changes must be applied before a service reloads them. Which approach best avoids unnecessary work while activating a coherent configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Reload after every file is copied, even when its contents are unchanged, to make each step independently visible.

options.label: B
options.text: Apply and validate the compatible changes, then reload once if relevant configuration actually changed.

options.label: C
options.text: Reload before changing the files, then skip the final reload if the configuration steps report success.

options.label: D
options.text: Apply all changes and avoid reloading while the service remains running, because a running process always reads updated settings.

grader_markdown: Apply and validate compatible changes before activation, then reload when relevant state changed. This avoids repeated reloads and allows the service to consume a coherent configuration. A running process does not necessarily reread changed files automatically.

title: Configuration success and functional success
prompt_markdown: All configuration steps report success, but users cannot use the application. Which interpretation and follow-up check are most useful?

options.label: A
options.text: Successful configuration proves the application works; compare automation exit codes from two consecutive runs.

options.label: B
options.text: The deployment must have drifted; check only whether all expected configuration files still exist.

options.label: C
options.text: A running service proves the application is reachable; compare installed package names with the deployment log.

options.label: D
options.text: Managed resources may be configured correctly while the user workflow still fails; exercise a representative request through the application and its dependencies.

grader_markdown: Configuration checks establish selected resource conditions, not necessarily end-to-end behavior. A representative request can expose failures in connectivity, dependencies, or application behavior that file, package, and process checks miss. Configuration success and functional failure can coexist.

title: Comparing codebase organizations
prompt_markdown: A growing team is considering replacing one large configuration file with reusable units and explicit environment composition. Which proposal best balances reuse with the cost of added structure?

options.label: A
options.text: Use coherent baseline and workload units with documented inputs and override rules; test their composition because extra interfaces can hide dependencies or conflicts.

options.label: B
options.text: Split every operation into its own unit and select them implicitly; the resulting file count makes ownership and effective configuration self-explanatory.

options.label: C
options.text: Copy each environment into its own repository; independent changes remove the need to coordinate common behavior across environments.

options.label: D
options.text: Keep one universal unit and add environment conditions throughout it; using one file removes the need to document how environment values interact.

grader_markdown: Coherent units support reuse and focused review, but extra interfaces and indirection can obscure dependencies and effective values. Documented inputs, visible composition, clear override rules, and integration checks address those costs. A small system may still be adequately served by a single file.

title: Checking the intended state
prompt_markdown: A deployment skips software setup whenever an 'application' directory exists. The directory remains after the desired version changes, so the process reports success without inspecting the version or behavior. Which correction best establishes the intended state?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the directory check and run the process twice; two unchanged runs establish that the desired version is installed.

options.label: B
options.text: Recreate the directory on every run and treat its new timestamp as proof that the application has been updated.

options.label: C
options.text: Compare the installed version or artifact with the desired one, repair missing or mismatched state, then verify the version and representative application behavior.

options.label: D
options.text: Update the deployment log with the desired version whenever the directory exists, then use that log as the check on future runs.

grader_markdown: Directory existence is not evidence of the desired software version or a complete installation. Repeated no-ops can preserve an incorrect state. Compare meaningful observed state with intended state, update when needed, and verify the result; changing a timestamp or log does not establish actual configuration.
